name: ABL Landscape Architecture
description: ABL Landscape Architecture is an award-winning, client-focused landscape architecture firm based in Lexington, Virginia offering expertise in institutional, civic, residential and commercial landscape architecture projects.
statement: ABL Landscape Architecture is principally devoted to the adaptation of historic, environmentally sensitive landscapes to contemporary needs and goals.

intro: The firm seeks to distill the essence of a site, and to respond to its innate character and context with creative, enduring design. ABL assists clients through all phases from initial concept to landscape establishment and maturation. We embrace open dialogue and exploration with clients, allied professionals, contractors, and end-users.

Mindful of the client's need to visualize the final product and also of the client's cost constraints in landscape construction and maintenance, ABL seeks every reasonable means to narrow the uncertainty between design incubation and the desired outcome. Such techniques include photo simulation, 3D scale models, material samples, full scale mock-ups, detailed review of pricing, dialogue with both grounds staff and end-users, and frequent site visits.
studio.note: ABL is a SWaM certified small business.

intro: ABL is a practice of three. The people a client meets first are the people who study the site, make the drawings and stay with the work, alongside the contractor, until it is built.

Its members have worked in Lexington and Rockbridge County for decades, with many of the same contractors, and they know which plants do well here. Arthur Bartenstein serves on the City of Lexington's Tree Committee and its Architectural Review Board and is president of the Rockbridge Historical Society. Kelly Morikawa, a certified arborist, owned and operated a landscape design, installation and maintenance company in the area for eighteen years.

The firm approaches a site as a preservationist does. It learns the story behind a place before it draws, so that the work is, in Arthur Bartenstein's words, "registered in terms of place, but also registered in terms of time." The design is then developed with the client, with the architects and engineers on the project, and with the people who will use and maintain the grounds.

The work ranges from private gardens to the Virginia Horse Center and the campuses of Washington and Lee University and the Virginia Military Institute. Before founding ABL, Arthur Bartenstein practiced with Peter Walker and Partners and the SWA Group in California and with Hill Studio in Roanoke and Frazier Associates in Staunton, on projects in Florida, California, Northern Virginia, Japan and China.

process.stepsIntro: A project begins with the three steps below. The firm then stays with it through design, construction and the establishment of the planting.

steps.title: First meeting
steps.text: The firm meets the client, hears what is wanted of the place and walks the site.

steps.title: Research
steps.text: The firm studies the land, the property and the area around it, and their history. For Courthouse Square in Lexington that meant the act of 1777 that created the county and called for a town at the seat of its court, and Court Day, the monthly session on which the county came to town to trade and talk.

steps.title: Brainstorming and mock-ups
steps.text: Ideas are worked out with the client in sketches, photo simulations and scale models. The chosen design is mocked up at full scale on the site, with samples of its materials, before it is built; Arthur Bartenstein calls the mock-up "the secret to getting good work."

services.intro: The firm researches every property it works on and mocks up what it designs, on a small job as on a large one. For a house, a garden or a farm it is engaged in one of four ways.
services.reviewNote: Service descriptions drafted by Claude from the November 11 meeting and rewritten the same day. The firm to confirm the scope of each and the wording.

items.name: Consultation
items.text: A visit to the property and the firm's recommendations for it.

items.name: Planting plan
items.text: A plan of what to plant and where, drawn by Kelly Morikawa and Bugs Utsey, who know which plants do well in this region.

items.name: Master plan
items.text: A design for the whole property: the research, the plan, drawings from which a contractor can build, and the firm's visits to the site until the work is finished.

items.name: Single elements
items.text: One part of a property, a stair for example, designed and seen through construction.
